Please answer this question with a number--which of the following best apply to the design in the study: 
        (1) totally fun first (i.e., Entertainment game reappropriated), 
        (2) mostly fun first (i.e., design workshop with disabled stakeholders),
        (3) both fun and utility first (i.e., design workshop with diverse stakeholders), 
        (4) mostly utility first (i.e., primary utilitarian mechanic designed first),
        (5) totally utility first (i.e., made by clinicians or specialists, fun incorporated later)
reasoning: The system (TIPS) is described as a novel computer-mediated communication technology explicitly designed to provide context-responsive ASL recommendations to improve sign language exposure and support parent autonomy, focusing on system latency, accuracy, and AR visualization. The emphasis is on a utilitarian communication-support mechanic (speech-driven ASL recommendation and projection-based AR) rather than on fun or entertainment design. Stakeholders mentioned are researchers, educators, parents, and DHH individuals, not framed as a fun-first game or entertainment repurposing. This aligns best with a mostly utility-first design where the primary utilitarian mechanic is designed first, with play as the context but not the design driver.

Please answer this question with a number--which of the following best apply to the design in the study: 
        (1) entirely skill-based (i.e., trivia, sports),
        (2) mostly skill-based (i.e., mario kart),
        (3) equally skill and chance-based (i.e., catan),
        (4) mostly chance-based (i.e., Uno),
        (5) entirely chance-based (i.e., all dice)
reasoning: The study is a system performance/usability evaluation of an AR-based ASL recommendation prototype during tabletop toy play. There is no game of chance, randomization, or probabilistic payoff structure; participants freely play with toys and speak, while the system detects objects and recommends ASL. Outcomes depend entirely on participants’ behavior and the system’s algorithms, not on random events. Thus, the design is best characterized as entirely skill-based within the provided scale.

        (4) most actions can be taken at any time, but there are some phases (i.e., PvP death reset timer),

reasoning: The study involves naturalistic joint play between a parent and child with toys on a tabletop, supported by an AR system that reacts in real time to the parent’s speech and toy interaction. There is no indication of discrete turns, ordered steps, or constrained phases; interaction appears continuous and overlapping, fitting an entirely simultaneous interaction structure.

        (1) entirely symmetrical (i.e., tic tac toe),
        (2) mostly symmetrical (i.e., undertale's differing NPC behaviors based on previous playthroughs),
        (3) both symmetrical and asymmetrical (i.e., pandemic with its similar turn structure but different character abilities),
        (4) mostly asymmetrical (i.e., tag),
        (5) entirely asymmetrical (i.e., keep talking, nobody explodes)
reasoning: The interaction is between a hearing parent and a DHH child, with the system monitoring only the parent’s speech and projecting ASL near objects of interest. Roles, information, and actions are fundamentally different for parent and child (one speaks and receives ASL prompts; the other receives signed input), making the setup fully asymmetrical rather than sharing any symmetric mechanics.
